title: Chan and Pure Land together
hookLine: in China and Vietnam many practice both: sitting and calling the name

cards: Sit in silence, or call the name? In a monastery in China, nobody is asked to choose. In the morning the meditation hall is silent; rows of monks and laypeople sit, nobody speaking, the incense burning down.

That afternoon, the same people are on their feet in another hall, walking slowly around an image of Amitabha, chanting Namo Amituofo, Amituofo, Amituofo, over and over. Nobody has switched schools at lunch.
Today: Chan and Pure Land together.

teach.h: SEPARATE IN JAPAN, ONE ROOF ELSEWHERE.
teach.b: First, where this happens. In Japan, Zen and Pure Land grew into separate schools with separate temples.
In China and Vietnam the story went differently: you can find monasteries and temples where sitting meditation and calling the name live side by side, practiced by the same people on the same day.
Vietnamese Thien, from the end of the Zen weeks, is one example. Second, a verse. Tradition credits a Chinese teacher, Yongming Yanshou, with a verse on the two practices.

teach.h: A TIGER THAT HAS GROWN HORNS.
teach.b: Its image: someone who has both Chan and Pure Land is like a tiger that has grown horns, strength with more strength added. Third, a question that joins them.

Some Chan teachers in China gave students who chant the name a question to hold: who is it that is reciting the Buddha's name? The chanting goes on, and underneath it the question turns back on the one chanting.
A Pure Land practice becomes a Chan question, and neither is dropped. Fourth, how practitioners describe the fit.

teach.h: SITTING QUIETS; THE NAME GIVES REST.
teach.b: Some say sitting quiets the mind, and the name gives it somewhere to rest.
Teachers don't all agree on how the two relate: some treat the name as the main practice and sitting as support, others the reverse.
But on an ordinary afternoon in a temple in Hanoi or Taipei, nobody needs to settle it first.

how: In some Chinese and Vietnamese monasteries and temples, practitioners combine sitting meditation with chanting Amitabha's name, sometimes holding the question 'who is reciting the Buddha's name?' while they chant.

games.q: what does “chan and pure land together” mean?
o: a Japanese school that merged Zen and Shin into one
sitting in silence and calling the name, in one temple
a rule that monks choose one practice and drop the other

games.q: you've sat in silence all morning. in the afternoon, the hall starts chanting Amitabha's name. what do you do?
o: leave: you belong to the sitting school.
join the chanting, the same practice day.
keep sitting and tell the others to be quiet.
games.why: in some Chinese and Vietnamese temples, the same people do both: sitting, then calling the name.

practice: For the first minute, just sit, feel the breath, and let the mind go quiet, the way it did in the Zen weeks.

Then, if you'd like, say Namo Amituofo softly, once on each out-breath, or listen to the name inside if you'd rather not chant. Once, partway through, ask quietly: who is saying this? Don't answer; keep going.

wordCard.voice: Chan and Pure Land together. In some temples in China and Vietnam, the same people sit in silence and call Amitabha's name: two practices under one roof. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese: who is it that recites the Buddha's name? a question joining Chan and Pure Land practice.

carryVoice: Your line: both together. A tiger that has grown horns. Go gently.
